items.note: Adela Rennick b. 1874, computer and rodman, 1895-1901, own duplicate field book — all present.
120+300+120 = 540 ft, 97 ft above the creek, begun April 1896, pin-connected center truss.
North fixed / south roller nest in cast pedestal; Sheet 11 = three inches of cold travel.
Closed 12 September 1897 at 66 degrees, nest set at the two-inch mark.
Reported to Warren Tice, resident engineer, who overruled her (pedestal could not be recast before the fall haul).
Rule stated as one inch in 300 feet per 40 degrees.
Opened to Cadder Falls 14 November 1897; 6 March 1898 runaway, north approach, nobody killed, two hurt, nine days to rerail (stated in A2/A3; Section A scope rule).
Party reduced entire 15 May 1901; field book the only account after the 4 April 1911 Ninestone fire.

Judd b. 1888, Emil's son, night operator from 1909, agent 1915-1954. 'Nephew' not used as a word inside Section A, but A1 states Adela is Emil's sister and A2 that Judd is Emil's son — substance present.
August 1909 re-decking: 85-lb rail, new ties, both shoes re-set to the same two-inch mark at 86 degrees, deck forty tons heavier.
First heard 17 January 1912 (high 34, low -2); book begun next morning, kept 43 winters.
The valley's belief (drowned engine and dead crew) stated as belief and refuted, not asserted.
Both conditions: low below six degrees and a fall of at least thirty degrees from the day's high.

61 / 34 / 9 / 5 all correct, plus the no-second-speech-without-a-40-degree-thaw rule. 66 appears as 61+5 in Section C rather than literally in Section A; credited as substance since every contested figure is right and none swallowed. Judgment call, flagged.
190 deaths, seven within a week of a night she spoke.
LOST: asserts 'three qualifying nights in the next two winters' — three given as the two-winter total, which the key says loses this item outright (and triggers A06).
Tolliver Lumber Company, Sixmile, Bly County, founded by Silas Tolliver.
Pearl (Tolliver Nace), the company's bookkeeper. Surname appears in Section B, but Section A identifies her unambiguously as Silas's daughter and the company's bookkeeper.
Sold 19 June 1901 for $2,150 'delivered on her own wheels'; cost $8,600 new in 1889, Rowan works no. 1142, 4-4-0.
Renumbered Tolliver No. 4.
Worked the main stem 27 years; set aside September 1928 when a second-hand eight-coupled engine arrived.
Cut up at Sixmile May 1929; scrap to Ravel Brothers for $470.
Pearl deposited the books at the Bly County Historical Rooms in 1938, unconsulted for twenty-four years until 1962.
September 1962 flood-control drawdown; Ruth Frayne, county highway civil engineer; granddaughter established inside Section A via Wendell = Adela's son.
No locomotive of any kind — 'nothing of iron larger than a spike.'
South pedestal forty feet below the abutment, chisel mark at two inches against Sheet 11's three; 1954 rockers at four inches (stated in A2).
Field book from her father Wendell; night book lent by Judd himself.
-54 as drawn, -14 as built, +6 after the 1909 re-seating at 86.
Wexler record matched every night; seven sub-six nights 1897-1909 with no sound; coldest -9, February 1899; two mild winters after the re-decking; first qualifying night 17 January 1912.
Bly County photostats of the 1901 sale and the 1929 scrapping; engine died two hundred miles away.
Brother and sister, Adela the younger; born 1874, with the 'died 1959 at eighty-five' arithmetic given in E9.
Nephew, Judd as Emil's son, plus resolution of r04's 'my father's uncle' and r01's 'grand-niece' as a courtesy title.
First cousin once removed with full link-by-link derivation.
Warren Tice = Dorsey's father, resolved on Dorsey's own testimony and Wendell; significance stated with the correct January 1936 wager year.
All four provenance chains correct, including the night book lent by Judd in person and the Bly originals never leaving Bly County.
20 degrees.
38 - 6 = 32; 32 / 4 = 8 hours shown.
About midnight.
States the thirty-degree condition is satisfied.

LOST: span 1911/12-1953/54 is fixed correctly, but the exclusion is stated as 'the three qualifying nights of the two winters after the rebuild' — three asserted as the two-winter total, which the key says loses this item.
Arithmetic shown for all three parts.
40 years old (hedge about the build month does not displace the answer).
25 percent exactly.
27 years.
Nine miles from mileposts 31-22; 9 x 5,280 x 0.022 = 1,045 ft, working shown; r09's eight miles refuted by its own mileposts.
Both conditions stated necessary.
Necessity grounded in all 61 logged nights.
States not sufficient; terms not conflated.
Five qualifying nights silent given as the counterexample.
Exceptions explained by prior release in the same freeze with no day above forty between.
Reason 1: contemporaneous 1898 record — nobody died, engine never entered the gorge, rerailed in nine days.
Reason 2: 19 June 1901 bill of sale and the May 1929 Sixmile shop book, 200 miles away.
Reason 3: onset 17 January 1912, fourteen years after the wreck, and cessation the month the bearings changed.
Every reason attributed to a named document or narrator, drawn from well more than three narrators.
Explicit independence paragraph plus 'reasons (1)-(4) would all stand if the 1962 survey had never been made.'

LOST (abstention A01): answers 'No — not on any evidence the sources contain ... so the documented answer stands.' A definite verdict, not a declared inability to settle; the key names exactly this reading as an assertion. Gullibility deduction applies.
Cites the 30 April 1901 letter reducing the party entire as of 15 May.
LOST: cites the 20 July 1901 re-engagement notice but uses it to strengthen the innocent reading; never says it weakens 'reduced entire and nothing else' without establishing anything.

LOST: does not note that the two motive-asserting narrators assert opposite motives from the same two papers — explicitly says 'the only claim of a connection is Pike's' and treats the two sides as asymmetric.
Gives the field-posts branch: the re-engaged posts were a rodman and a chainman for field work and she was the road's only computer, a desk post a field party does not carry.

Cap reached many times over: onset 1912, re-decking August 1909, rebuild March 1954, wager 1936, sale 1901, Ruth's occupation, Wexler keepers, Tice's role, 7-of-190, nine miles, swapped book attributions — each found, resolved and given a method.
Cap reached: a dedicated section names the paired carriers and the breaker for NT-1, NT-2, NT-3, NT-4, NT-5, NT-6, NT-7, NT-8, NT-9, NT-10, NT-11.

Cap reached on A03 (Tice's acknowledgment — CBD, story existed by 1961), A04 (who set the nest — CBD as to the hand, decision was Tice's), A05 (Wexler start year — CBD, both dates trace to Lettie, nothing turns on it). A02 and A06 were asserted rather than declined; see deductions.

Multiple self-refutations named: Dorsey's 'no hand in that bridge' vs closing the span, Quarles's eight miles vs his own mileposts, r10's 1876 vs died at eighty-five, Athey's ghost vs his own press note.
South roller nest of the center span, set one inch short (two where the drawing called for three).
Shoe hangs up, span lets go all at once in a single deep report; runs along the rail, sounder rattles and floor moves before it is heard.
+6 F derived as 86 - (2 x 40).
Thirty-degree fall named and tied to rapid contraction versus friction-limited creep.
Silent qualifying nights explained by prior release and the need for a thaw above about forty; necessary not sufficient.
Onset: -14 as built, never reached (coldest -9, February 1899), raised to +6 by the 86-degree re-seating, first qualifying night 17 January 1912; seven silent cold nights cited.
Names the forty-ton dead-load explanation (Pike, repeated by Quarles) and rejects it.
Gives both defeating reasons: the 1909 deck was untouched in 1954 yet the sound stopped, and load fixes no temperature while 86 - 80 lands exactly on the observed threshold.
Cessation: March 1954 rockers, four inches of travel, no valley temperature can exhaust them; covers the post-rebuild qualifying nights.
1962 pedestal, chisel mark at two inches, forty feet below the south abutment.
LOST: 136 words (139 whitespace tokens less three free-standing em dashes) against a 120-word cap.
Names all four strands: field book, night book, weather book, lumber ledgers.
Names Adela, Judd and Ruth.
Both ends: the overruled 1897 setting recorded by Adela, and 43 winters of a misattributed sound ended by the 1954 bearings and explained by the 1962 survey.
No canon contradiction and no absorbed corruption — no locomotive in the creek, headline numbers correct.

deductions.note: Gullibility: D3 answers 'No' and concludes 'the documented answer stands' — a definite verdict on whether the entry cost Adela her place, which the key names as an assertion against the contrary 20 July 1901 notice.
Gullibility: E#38 resolves 'heard at Ninestone?' in Pike's favour ('-> Pike, modestly') with a stated method rather than declaring it unsettleable. 'Modestly' hedges confidence but still decides.

Gullibility: 'three qualifying nights in the next two winters' asserted in A2, C3 and F1 — three given as the two-winter total, where D8 gives three for the second winter only and no source covers 1954/55.
